newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-DELY VALDES HOPES TO LINK UP AGAIN WITH TABAREZ.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DELY VALDES HOPES TO LINK UP AGAIN WITH TABAREZ.

text.p: Panama's veteran striker Julio Cesar Dely Valdes could link up with Uruguayan former AC Milan coach Oscar Washington Tabarez, his boss at Cagliari two years ago, if the pair both join Spanish club Oviedo in the coming season.
"There's nothing concrete yet. I'm waiting. Tabarez hasn't signed yet but if he does in the coming days then there's a good chance it could come off," the Paris St Germain striker said on Wednesday.
Tabarez lost his job at AC Milan last December when he was replaced by former Italy manager Arrigo Sacchi.
"I'm hopeful. I'd like to go to Spain, there's the language too. Let's hope something happens in the next few days," Dely Valdes said in an interview.

Dely Valdes has been told by his French club, runners-up in the first division last season, that he can leave after failing to command a regular first-team place in the second of his two seasons in Paris.
This was in marked contrast to his 15 goals in 33 games in the 1995-6 season and prolific goalscoring with Nacional of Montevideo before his move to Cagliari in Italy in 1993.
He has remained in the French capital to sort out his future while the PSG squad have left town for pre-season training.
Dely Valdes, 30, has also been looking at the possibility of a move to Japan where his twin brother Jorge now plays.
"It's difficult now, they're already playing their championship but it's not impossible. I liked the idea of finishing my career close to my brother," he said.
Dely Valdes comes from a pioneering family in Panamanian football, having followed his elder brother Armando to Argentina in the late 1980s.
Armando was the first player from his country to venture beyond the limited confines of Central American football into a major sphere in the game. He now coaches in his home country.
The twins soon followed to Argentina, where Julio Cesar played for Diego Maradona's first club Argentinos Juniors, before they branched out to Uruguay and Chile respectively.
